meta.regime: Every price on this page is Friday's close and every price on this page is wrong, because the event that decided the week happened on Saturday after the market shut. Friday traded a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz: WTI fell 2.33% to 92.410, Brent 2.14% to 104.320, the DAX rose 0.56% and the franc did nothing. On Saturday President Trump rejected Iran's seven-day roadmap at the White House - 'That deal would not be acceptable' - and the Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the November midterms. The invalidation this page named on Friday has fired in full, so the board resets: the four central banks whose hawkishness was conditioned on expensive energy get their condition back, the petro-currency gets its terms of trade back, the franc gets its haven bid back, and oil opens Monday having spent Friday pricing a deal that is dead.

dailyRead: This is a Sunday report and the single most useful thing it can do is tell you that the tape you are looking at is stale. Friday's close was built on one story: Iranian and US negotiators had held side talks at the UN General Assembly on a phased reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had conveyed a concrete seven-day plan through Qatar, and the market took the de-escalation at face value - WTI down 2.33% to 92.410, Brent down 2.14% to 104.320, gasoline down 4.80%, the DAX up 0.56% to 25409 and the Euro Stoxx 50 up 0.41% to 6298. On Saturday President Trump killed it. Speaking to reporters at the White House he said the offer was not acceptable - 'That deal would not be acceptable' - added that Iran wants a deal because 'they are losing so badly' and that on closing the strait 'they outsmarted themselves', and the Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the US midterm elections in November. Araghchi replied on Telegram that Iran stands by its conditions and that 'only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock'. Al Jazeera's correspondent called the proposal dead in the water. Yesterday this page wrote that the invalidation for the whole de-escalation trade was a single headline - talks breaking down, as they did after the June 17 memorandum - and that headline arrived roughly eighteen hours later, after the close. So the honest structure of today's report is that six of eight currency scores move, three of them straight back to where they were on Thursday, and the reason is one fact rather than eight. Start with the cleanest consequence. USOIL flips from SHORT to LONG: Friday's 2.33% fall discounted a deal that no longer exists, independent trackers put Hormuz throughput at 3.7 to 8m b/d against roughly 20m normally, and the Houthis spent Thursday firing six ballistic missiles at Taif and the Yanbu area, which the Saudi-led coalition intercepted - Yanbu being the main alternative route for Saudi crude, fed by an East-West pipeline that can carry up to seven million barrels a day. An attack on the bypass while the strait is shut is a different supply picture than an attack on the strait alone, and a stated expectation of renewed bombing after November gives the risk premium a date rather than removing it. The second consequence is Canadian and it is the biggest single reversal on this page. Twenty-four hours ago CAD was the weakest currency here at -1, and the explicit reason was that falling crude weakened Canada's terms of trade and pushed Governor Macklem's hawkish conditional - written against the US$100 level - back out of reach. Brent is 104.320 and the direction of travel has inverted, so that argument inverts with it. CAD goes to 0. What keeps it from going further is genuinely weak domestic data that the oil price does not touch: August employment -41.7k after +75.1k, the only contracting PMIs on this board at 46.8 services and 47.8 composite, and monthly GDP on Tuesday at 12:30Z where consensus is 0.1% against 0.3%. USD/CAD stays long because of a 175bp rate gap, but it drops from HIGH to LOW-MED conviction because the leg that was yesterday's tailwind is now a headwind. Third, the franc. CHF went to -1 on Friday as the purest expression of de-escalation; a war that is being re-escalated on a schedule is exactly when the franc bids, so CHF returns to 0. The structural short case is untouched - the SNB policy rate is 0.00% for a third consecutive assessment, the conditional inflation forecast assumes zero across the entire horizon to 2029, June's stated willingness to intervene against appreciation has been replaced by symmetric standby wording, inflation is 0.8%, and Swiss CPI on Thursday is forecast at 0.0% m/m against 0.4% - but a zero-rate haven in a widening war is a 0, not a -1. Fourth, the euro, and this is where the correction matters most because it reverses a call this page made yesterday. EUR was cut from +1 to 0 on the argument that cheaper crude undercut the inflation leg while German GfK consumer climate at -30.6 undercut the growth leg. The growth leg is unchanged and still bad. The inflation leg was simply wrong, and the data says so independently of Trump: euro-area energy inflation accelerated to 14.3% y/y in August from 10.3% in July, the September flash estimate on Friday October 2 carries a consensus of 3.7% headline against 3.2% released and 2.5% core, and German preliminary CPI on Wednesday is forecast at 0.5% m/m against 0.2%. An inflation-targeting central bank looking at a 3.7% print does not stop because a survey was weak. EUR goes back to +1, with October 29 pricing near a coin flip - one read has 53% for no change - and Lagarde speaking three times this week. Fifth, sterling. Bailey's hawkishness is the most explicitly energy-conditioned on this board: he said on Friday it is 'going to get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices'. Read that with Brent rising rather than falling and the November 5 case, roughly 75% priced with three of nine already voting to hike in September, is re-armed rather than undermined. GBP goes to +2, and Bailey speaks again on Thursday at 08:00Z. The risk is fiscal, not monetary - the October 28 Budget with borrowing 8.1bn above the OBR profile against a gilt 10-year at 5.3528, the highest yield of the majors and not the good kind. Sixth, and this is the correction that matters for the week's biggest trade: Australia. This page has argued for days that the RBA case is the one hawkish case that does not depend on the oil price at all, and that was the entire reason to own AUD into de-escalation. That was wrong, and Governor Bullock said so herself - she told a parliamentary committee that some of the upside inflation risks flagged in August appear to be materialising, and the driver reported alongside that was the rise in global oil prices amid the Middle East conflict, with Brent climbing from around US$80 to above US$100. So the Australian case is energy-exposed like the others. The difference is that today energy is going the hawkish way, which means the re-escalation reinforces the RBA instead of being irrelevant to it, and the domestic case is stacked on top rather than instead: trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% against a 2-3% band, and a monthly CPI on Wednesday with TE consensus at 4.1% against 3.5%. Add the highest bond yield of the majors at 5.385 and a copper market in genuine physical squeeze - LME available metal down to 133,725 tonnes with 115,450 of 255,900 tonnes on cancelled warrants, the Yangshan premium at US$124 a tonne, the highest in almost four years, and the cash-to-three-month spread swung from an US$86 discount to a premium - and AUD goes to +3. Respect the sequencing though: at 92-94% priced the hike is not the trade, and a cautious statement on Tuesday followed by a soft CPI on Wednesday is a two-step sell-the-fact. Seventh, New Zealand goes to -1, and this is a relative call rather than a new fact. TE's calendar carries October 28 as an explicit hold at 2.75% with the hike to 3.0% at December 9, the economy is the most conflicted here with inflation at 4.1% but unemployment rising to 5.6% and wage growth of only 2.1%, and NZD is the worst major on the month at -4.76%. Governor Breman's warning that crude could push inflation higher is re-armed by escalation, which is the one thing working for it, and it is not enough against a central bank that has moved its own hike six weeks out. Eighth, the dollar and the yen both hold, and both for reasons worth reading. USD stays +2: the Fed is at 4.00%, composite PMI 58.4 is the strongest since July 2021, and higher oil is ambiguous rather than negative for it. But this is the week the invalidation gets tested properly, because non-farm payrolls on Friday carry a TE consensus of 100K against 162K previous with TE's own model at 90K, alongside core PCE on Wednesday forecast at 0.3% m/m from 0.2%. Accelerating core inflation with decelerating payrolls into a consumer already at a 48.1 sentiment reading is the definition of a stagflationary print, and October pricing near 67-70% has room to fall. JPY stays 0 and the reason to read it is another correction: yesterday this page said the risk on Tokyo CPI was skewed toward a soft print. The calendar says the opposite - Tokyo core CPI on Thursday at 23:30Z carries a consensus of 2.4% y/y against 1.8% previous, which is a large acceleration and would put a December BoJ hike back in play. Against that, Japan is the purest energy importer here and rising crude is a terms-of-trade tax, so the two cancel and the yen stays a range. What does not cancel is the intervention line: Finance Minister Katayama said the principles behind the July 31 joint US-Japan intervention are still alive and authorities checked rates with dealers before the weekend, so 160 is defended and USD/JPY is a 157-160 range rather than a trend. Metals get a new leg. Gold at 4285.00 and silver at 64.259 spent the week losing 2.25% and 2.99% because a 2.84% ten-year TIPS real yield against a 5.165 nominal is punitive carry, and that has not changed - but escalation with a stated date restores the premium that was leaking out, so both go long at low conviction rather than staying flat. Equities go the other way: GER40 short at medium, because Friday's 0.56% gain was explicitly attributed to reopening optimism and it is the index most exposed to German gas and a re-armed hawkish ECB. EU50 is short too but at lower conviction and for a different reason, which is the point of scoring it separately - banks are its heaviest sector, so a Bund at 3.621 and an ECB facing a 3.7% flash print support the weight that GER40 does not have, and that cushions the index rather than saving it. The cleanest trades, and the honest ranking: AUD/NZD long at high conviction remains the best ticket because it is a four-point gap between two hiking central banks whose calendars are six weeks apart and it needs no view on the barrel; GBP/NZD long and EUR/NZD long express the same re-armed energy hawkishness against the weakest of them; AUD/CHF and GBP/CHF long hold up because a zero rate loses to a hiking one even with a haven bid; and USOIL long is the direct expression, sized for the fact that Qatar is still mediating and Araghchi is still waiting on official channels rather than on Trump's press remarks. What to be careful with: everything on this page assumes Monday opens where Friday closed, and it will not. The gap is the risk and the opportunity, and the pairs whose thesis rests on a central bank calendar rather than on a barrel are the ones that survive a gap in either direction.

today.headline: Trump's rejection of Iran's Hormuz roadmap turns the leg that was shorting CAD into a leg that supports it, with USD/CAD at 1.41421
today.read: UP from -1 to 0, and this is the largest single reversal on the page. Read yesterday's entry alongside it, because the logic is being inverted rather than adjusted: CAD was the weakest currency here explicitly because Brent falling to 104.320 weakened Canada's terms of trade while pushing Governor Macklem's hawkish conditional, framed against the US$100 level, out of reach. On Saturday President Trump rejected Iran's seven-day plan to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, and the Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects a renewed bombing campaign after the November midterms. Crude's direction of travel inverts, so both halves invert with it. What keeps CAD at 0 rather than positive is that nothing domestic improved and the barrel cannot fix any of it: August employment -41.7k after +75.1k, the only contracting PMIs on this board at 46.8 services and 47.8 composite, July core retail sales -0.7% against -0.5% expected with volumes down 1.1%, and a rate frozen at 2.25% since before September 2 at a 175bp discount to the Fed. Forward, the immediate test is monthly GDP on Tuesday at 12:30Z, forecast at 0.1% against 0.3% - a miss there would reassert the domestic story against the commodity one. Then the Business Outlook Survey on October 19 and the Monetary Policy Report on October 28, where the oil price assumption is now the thing to read. Practical read: USD/CAD stays long on the rate gap but drops to LOW-MED conviction, AUD/CAD comes off HIGH to MED, and NZD/CAD short is the cleaner way to be short a weak antipodean than to be short Canada.

today.headline: The franc's haven bid returns on a war being re-escalated to a schedule, with USD/CHF at 0.82827 after a 2.83% monthly climb

Yesterday CHF was cut to -1 as the purest expression of de-escalation, on the argument that a haven which would not bid during a missile salvo had even less reason to bid into reopening talks. Those talks are dead: Trump called the offer not acceptable on Saturday, Araghchi replied on Telegram that Iran stands by its conditions and that 'only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock', and the reported expectation of a renewed bombing campaign after the November midterms gives the escalation a date. That is a haven input, and it is why the -1 does not survive the weekend. Everything structural is unchanged and still argues the other way: the SNB policy rate is 0.00% for a third consecutive assessment, the conditional inflation forecast assumes zero across the entire horizon to 2029, June's stated willingness to intervene against appreciation has been replaced by symmetric standby wording, Schlegel described a roughly 3% trade-weighted depreciation as in line with rate differentials without objecting to it, and inflation is 0.8% with core 0.4%. Swiss CPI on Thursday at 06:30Z is forecast at 0.0% m/m from 0.4%, and Schlegel speaks the same day at 15:30Z. Forward: a zero-rate haven in a widening war is a 0, not a positive, because it bids on headlines and loses carry every day in between. Practical read: CHF crosses stay short against every hiking central bank - AUD/CHF and GBP/CHF long - but conviction comes down a notch and CAD/CHF becomes a range rather than a directional ticket.

today.headline: The euro returns to +1 within a day, because the inflation leg cut on Friday was cut on an input that both Trump and the data have now reversed
today.read: UP from 0 back to +1, and this is a correction of this page's own call rather than a response to a new print, so it is worth being explicit about what changed. Yesterday EUR was cut from +1 to 0 on two arguments: cheaper crude undercut the inflation leg, and German GfK consumer climate at -30.6 undercut the growth leg. The growth leg stands entirely - GfK printed -30.6 against -27.4 expected from a revised -26.8, with income expectations collapsing from +1.7 to -15.0 and willingness to save rising from 15.5 to 21.5, all attributed to energy costs. The inflation leg was wrong on two counts. First, it rested on a Hormuz reopening that Trump rejected on Saturday. Second, and more importantly, the released data was already pointing the other way: euro-area energy inflation accelerated to 14.3% y/y in August from 10.3% in July, which is pass-through arriving with a lag rather than fading. The calendar now confirms it - the September flash estimate on Friday October 2 at 09:00Z carries a consensus of 3.7% headline against the 3.2% released, with core at 2.5% from 2.4%, and German preliminary CPI on Wednesday is forecast at 0.5% m/m from 0.2%. An inflation-targeting Governing Council facing 3.7% does not stand down because a consumer survey was poor. Forward: the deposit rate is 2.50% after September 10, October 29 pricing is near a coin flip with one read putting no change at 53%, and Lagarde speaks three times this week - Monday 13:30Z, Tuesday 11:00Z, Thursday 13:30Z. That coin flip is exactly why EUR returns to +1 and no higher. Practical read: EUR/USD stays short on the rate gap, EUR/NZD goes long, EUR/CAD long comes down in conviction, and EUR/AUD stays short into Tuesday.

today.headline: The RBA is Tuesday at 04:30Z not Monday, and monthly CPI the day after carries a 4.1% consensus against 3.5% previous
today.read: UP to +3, the strongest currency on this board, with two corrections attached. The first is calendar: this page has said Monday September 29 for a week and the day is Tuesday - TE and ForexFactory both time the decision at 04:30Z on September 29, with a press conference at 05:30Z. The second is analytical and more important. This page argued for days that the Australian hawkish case was the only one here that did not rest on the oil price, and made that the reason to own AUD into de-escalation. Governor Bullock contradicted that herself: she told a parliamentary committee that some of the upside inflation risks flagged in August appear to be materialising, and the driver reported alongside was the rise in global oil prices amid the Middle East conflict, with Brent climbing from around US$80 to above US$100. Australia is energy-exposed like the others. What makes that a feature today rather than a problem is direction - Saturday's escalation pushes the RBA the same way the domestic data does. And the domestic data stands on its own: trimmed mean stuck at 3.6% against a 2-3% band with the decline stalled, Q2 GDP at 2.1% y/y above expectations, August employment +39,493 after -15,864, against unemployment at 4.6% from 4.5% as the one softening series. TE carries Previous 4.35% with consensus and forecast both at 4.60%, all four major banks agree, and 92-94% is priced. Copper adds the second leg: LME available metal down to 133,725 tonnes with 115,450 of 255,900 tonnes on cancelled warrants, the Yangshan premium at US$124 a tonne - the highest in almost four years - and the cash-to-three-month spread swung from an US$86 discount into premium. Forward, respect the sequencing: monthly CPI lands Wednesday at 01:30Z with TE consensus 4.1% and TE's own model 4.0% against 3.5% previous, so the Bank hikes into a print it has not seen and CBA has flagged that a hot Q3 could take the rate to 4.85%. A cautious statement Tuesday followed by a soft CPI Wednesday is a two-step sell-the-fact into a currency already down 1.38% on the week. Practical read: express this in crosses rather than against the dollar - AUD/NZD at 1.24034 is the cleanest ticket on the page.

today.headline: New Zealand drops to -1 without a single new data point, because the board around it strengthened while its own central bank moved six weeks further out
today.read: DOWN from 0 to -1, and the honest description is a relative downgrade rather than a new fact, which is worth saying plainly. TE's calendar carries October 28 at 01:00Z with Previous 2.75% and a TEForecast of 2.75% - an explicit hold - with the hike to 3.0% sitting at December 9. That puts the next RBNZ move six weeks behind the RBA's, and on a board where sterling and the euro both just recovered their hawkish legs, standing still is falling behind. Reported market pricing remains genuinely contradictory here - one read has at least 75% for 3% on October 28, another has 88% for no change - and because that cannot be resolved from the available sources this page carries TE's hold call and states the disagreement rather than burying it. Governor Breman's warning that near-term inflation could overshoot if higher crude persists is the one argument Saturday's escalation restores, and on its own it is not enough. The underlying data is the most internally conflicted on this board: inflation at 4.1% is the highest of these eight economies and rising from 3.1%, while unemployment climbs to 5.6% from 5.4%, wage growth is only 2.1% and GDP rebounded to 2.6% y/y. That combination - the highest inflation and a deteriorating labour market - is what makes the RBNZ's own hesitation credible. NZD is the worst major on the month at -4.76% against the dollar. Forward: Q3 CPI in mid-October and the unemployment rate decide December, and there is no domestic catalyst this week at all, so NZD trades as the funding leg of other people's stories. Practical read: AUD/NZD long at high conviction, GBP/NZD and EUR/NZD long, NZD/CAD short.

today.headline: Bailey's hawkishness is explicitly conditioned on expensive energy, and after Saturday that condition is working for sterling instead of against it
today.read: UP from +1 to +2, and the upgrade is the mirror image of yesterday's warning. Bailey said on Friday at the Oxford / New York Fed / Bank of England conference that the Bank has not increased Bank Rate and that it is 'going to get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices', adding that the Bank cannot wait for the full evidence of energy feeding into inflation expectations while describing that evidence so far as 'quite subdued'. Yesterday this page called that the single biggest liability on the board, because no other central bank had tied its turn to a price that was falling. Trump rejected Iran's roadmap on Saturday and the Houthis spent Thursday firing on Yanbu, so the condition is now being satisfied rather than undermined, and what was a liability becomes a commitment. TE's own vote rows confirm the base: Bank Rate 3.75% held on September 17 with BoE MPC Vote Hike 3/9 and Vote Cut 0/9, so three members already want to tighten, with Lombardelli and Breeden having moved on the same conditional logic that Bailey ratified. November 5 is roughly 75% priced. Forward, the risk has moved from monetary to fiscal and that matters for how to hold this: the October 28 Budget arrives with borrowing running 8.1bn above the OBR profile against a gilt 10-year at 5.3528, the highest yield of the majors - a term-premium yield rather than a policy one, which means a loosening Budget could weaken sterling on the same week the MPC turns hawkish. Bailey speaks again Thursday at 08:00Z and the Financial Policy Committee record lands Wednesday at 09:30Z. Composite PMI 51.7, inflation 3.1% with core 2.6%, unemployment 4.9%, employment change +67k from +83k, wage growth cooling to 3.9% from 4.2%. Practical read: express sterling against the weak rather than against the dollar - GBP/NZD and GBP/CHF long, GBP/USD a range.

today.headline: No new dollar data over the weekend, but the week ahead is built to test the invalidation this page named: payrolls Friday with a 100K consensus against 162K
today.read: HOLDS +2 and stays the second-strongest currency here, with the composition of the coming week mattering more than anything that happened in the last two days. The level is unchanged and still strong: the Fed funds upper bound is 4.00% after a unanimous September 16 hike, composite PMI at 58.4 is the strongest since July 2021, DXY closed at 100.971 down 0.31% but up 0.75% on the week and 1.82% on the month, and the 10-year sits at 5.165 with the TIPS real yield at 2.84%. What is different is that the invalidation gets a real test rather than another sentiment survey. Core PCE lands Wednesday September 30 at 12:30Z forecast at 0.3% m/m against 0.2%, with final GDP at 1.5%. Non-farm payrolls land Friday October 2 at 12:30Z with TE consensus at 100K against 162K previous and TE's own model at 90K, unemployment forecast unchanged at 4.1% and average hourly earnings at 0.3%. Core inflation accelerating while hiring decelerates by roughly a third, into a household already at a 48.1 sentiment reading with year-ahead inflation expectations at 4.6%, is the stagflationary print this page has been describing as the trigger - and October pricing near 67-70% has room to fall without the dollar losing its yield advantage. Saturday's escalation is ambiguous for the dollar rather than negative: higher crude feeds the inflation side that argues for October while taxing the consumption side that argues against, and it adds a haven bid that the DXY captures. Forward: CB consumer confidence and JOLTS on Tuesday at 14:00Z, ADP Wednesday, ISM manufacturing and Waller on Thursday, then the minutes on October 7 and the decision on October 28, where the September SEP has the dots stopping at 4.1% for both 2026 and 2027. Practical read: stay long the dollar against the weak antipodean and short it against the hiking Australian.

today.headline: USD/JPY holds 157.252 with 160 defended, and the Tokyo CPI consensus of 2.4% against 1.8% reverses what this page said about the risk on that print
today.read: HOLDS 0, and the reason to read this entry is a correction. Yesterday this page wrote that the risk on Tokyo CPI was skewed toward a soft print, partly because cheaper crude would cut imported inflation. Both halves of that have turned over. The calendar carries Tokyo core CPI on Thursday October 1 at 23:30Z with a consensus of 2.4% y/y against 1.8% previous - a substantial acceleration that would put a December BoJ hike back into play rather than out of it - and crude is rising again after Trump's rejection rather than falling. Against that, Japan is the purest energy importer on this board, so a re-escalating Hormuz is a direct terms-of-trade tax on the yen even as it lifts the inflation the Bank is normalising into. Those two forces roughly cancel, which is why JPY stays at 0 and stays a range rather than becoming a trend in either direction. What does not cancel is officialdom, and that is the tradeable part. USD/JPY fell 1.02% to 157.252 on Friday as the 158.30 break failed; Finance Minister Katayama said the principles behind the joint US-Japan intervention of July 31 remain alive; Japanese authorities checked rates with dealers in overseas markets before the weekend, historically the step that precedes action; and macro desks cut leveraged short-yen carry into that tail rather than test it. Policy itself is unchanged: the rate is 1.25% after September 18 and TE carries an explicit 1.25% hold for October 30 alongside the Quarterly Outlook Report, with the Summary of Opinions landing Wednesday at 23:50Z. Board member Masu said hikes continue with the pace hinging on the July baseline and on risks from crude, AI demand and FX. Headline CPI 1.9% with core 1.7%, wage growth 4.7%, unemployment 2.4%, GDP 0.7% y/y. Practical read: 160 is defended and 157 is the carry floor, so trade the 157-160 range, hold XXX/JPY longs at reduced conviction, and treat Thursday night's print as the event that could break it.

catalysts.event: RBA cash rate decision and rate statement - Reserve Bank of Australia
catalysts.note: The event of the quarter, and note the day: Tuesday, not Monday, which this page had wrong for a week. ForexFactory's red folder carries Cash Rate and RBA Rate Statement at 04:30Z with forecast 4.60% against 4.35% previous; TE's calendar carries Previous 4.35%, consensus 4.60% and TEForecast 4.60%. All four major Australian banks forecast the hike and market pricing is 92-94%. The case: trimmed mean inflation stuck at 3.6% against a 2-3% band with the decline stalled, headline 3.5%, Q2 GDP at 2.1% y/y above expectations, August employment +39,493, against unemployment at 4.6% from 4.5% as the one softening series. Governor Bullock told a parliamentary committee that some of the upside inflation risks flagged in August appear to be materialising, with the rise in global oil prices reported as a driver - which is why Saturday's escalation reinforces this rather than bypassing it. Because the hike is 92-94% priced, the tradeable content is the statement and any guidance on whether 4.60% is terminal. A hike takes Australia to the highest policy rate of the majors, 60bp above the Fed's upper bound and 210bp above the ECB deposit rate.

catalysts.event: Australia CPI y/y, CPI m/m and trimmed mean CPI m/m - ABS
catalysts.note: The most awkward sequencing on the page: this lands the morning AFTER the RBA decides, so the Bank hikes into a print it has not seen. ForexFactory's red folders carry CPI y/y forecast 4.1% against 3.5% previous, CPI m/m 0.5% against 1.0%, and trimmed mean CPI m/m 0.3% against 0.5%. A 4.1% print would make Australian headline inflation the highest of these eight economies, level with New Zealand and rising, and CBA has noted a hot Q3 reading could take the cash rate to 4.85%. The asymmetry is what matters for AUD: a print at or above 4.1% validates Tuesday and extends the path, while anything at or below 3.5% turns a 92-94% priced hike into a policy error and is the cleanest sell-the-fact setup on this page.

Read it as the first half of a two-part test: this print carries the inflation side of the stagflation question and Friday's payrolls carry the labour side. A 0.3% core PCE followed by a payrolls print at 90-100K against 162K previous is the combination that gives the committee no clean answer and is the specific mix this page has named as the dollar's invalidation - not because it is dollar-negative on its own, but because it caps how far the Fed can extend beyond the 4.1% median dot.

October pricing near 67-70% has room to fall on a weak print, and the September SEP caps the path at a 4.1% median for both 2026 and 2027 regardless. Watch the unemployment rate as much as the headline: a move above 4.1% would be the first genuine labour crack after two false starts.

Watch it against a defended 160 in USD/JPY and a 157 carry floor.

catalysts.event: Euro-area flash CPI and core CPI y/y - Eurostat
catalysts.note: At 09:00Z, forecast 3.7% headline and 2.5% core - and this is the single most important input into an October 29 ECB decision that reported pricing puts near a coin flip at about 53% for no change. catalysts.event: Iran / US war - Trump rejects the seven-day Hormuz roadmap
catalysts.note: The single most important item on this page and the reason six of eight currency scores moved today. On Saturday September 26 President Trump rejected Iran's proposal at the White House - 'That deal would not be acceptable' - saying Iran wants a deal because 'they are losing so badly' and that on closing the strait 'they outsmarted themselves'. The Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the US midterm elections in November. Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi had conveyed a concrete seven-day plan through Qatar requiring the US to lift its naval blockade, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen assets and observe a ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen, with the strait reopening on day seven; he replied on Telegram that Iran stands by its conditions and that 'only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock'. Al Jazeera's correspondent described the proposal as dead in the water. Why this is the whole report: Friday's close priced the opposite outcome, with WTI down 2.33% to 92.410 and Brent down 2.14% to 104.320, so every level on this page predates the news. Independent trackers put Hormuz throughput at 3.7-8m b/d against roughly 20m normally, around 20% of global seaborne oil trade. The two-way risk is that Qatar is still mediating and this same channel produced the June 17 memorandum, so a resumption can arrive as abruptly as the rejection did.

catalysts.event: Houthi missile attacks on Saudi Arabia - Yanbu and the East-West pipeline
catalysts.note: The escalation that makes the Hormuz closure worse rather than merely longer. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted six ballistic missiles on Thursday aimed at Taif in western Saudi Arabia and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea; the Houthis then claimed attacks on a sensitive target in Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities in Yanbu, with spokesman Yahya Saree saying ballistic and cruise missiles and drones were used. Damage was not confirmed, and a widespread emergency alert covered areas including Jeddah and Mecca. Yanbu matters because it is the main alternative route for Saudi crude, fed by an East-West pipeline that can carry up to seven million barrels a day - the designated bypass for a closed strait. Attacking the bypass while the strait is shut is a materially different supply picture, and it is part of why USOIL flips long.

catalysts.event: Japanese FX intervention risk near 160 - Ministry of Finance / Bank of Japan

Finance Minister Katayama said the principles behind the joint US-Japan intervention of July 31 are still alive; Japanese authorities checked rates with dealers in overseas markets before the weekend, historically a precursor to action; and USD/JPY fell 1.02% to 157.252 on Friday as the 158.30 break failed and macro desks cut leveraged short-yen carry rather than test it. Treat 160 as defended and 157 as the carry floor: XXX/JPY longs are held at reduced conviction and USD/JPY is a range rather than a trend. Thursday's Tokyo core CPI at a forecast 2.4% is the print that could break it from the other side.

catalysts.event: Copper physical squeeze - LME stocks and the Yangshan premium
catalysts.note: The supply story behind the XCU long and a second-order support for AUD. Of 255,900 tonnes in LME warehouses, 115,450 - about 45% - are cancelled warrants already earmarked for removal, leaving readily available metal at 133,725 tonnes; Comex now holds roughly 69% of global exchange copper stocks after eighteen months of tariff-driven flows. The cash-to-three-month spread has swung from an US$86 discount in mid-September into premium, the sharpest nearby backwardation since 2021, and the Yangshan premium at Shanghai's principal import hub reached US$124 a tonne, the highest in almost four years. The near-term caveat is demand timing: China's October 1-7 holiday pauses the restocking that drove last week's five-session rally.

catalysts.event: US-China trade truce extended to January 10 - US Treasury
catalysts.note: Bessent confirmed a two-month extension of the truce that was due to expire November 10, taking it to January 10, during Xi's state visit to Washington. Markets had expected six months or longer, and the short extension was read as Washington keeping the heat on, with little progress on AI, Iran or Taiwan. Modestly risk-positive and copper-supportive - relevant mainly as a second-order support for the XCU long and therefore for AUD.

geopolitics: The de-escalation trade died on Saturday, and because it died after the close, every price on this page is a price for a world that no longer exists. Take the sequence exactly as it happened, because the timing is the trade. Through Thursday and Friday the market was told that a settlement was close: Iranian and US negotiators held side talks on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly, Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi conveyed a concrete seven-day plan through Qatar, and Pakistan's Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif used his UNGA address to publicise Islamabad's mediation. The plan was specific: the United States would lift its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waive sanctions on Iranian oil sales, release an estimated $12bn in frozen Iranian assets and observe a ceasefire covering Lebanon and Yemen; Araghchi estimated four or five days to satisfy the conditions, reopening on day seven, with talks on a final deal beginning the same day. The market bought it. WTI fell 2.33% to 92.410 and Brent 2.14% to 104.320, gasoline fell 4.80%, European gas fell 3.06% to 3.1960, the DAX rose 0.56% to 25409 with TradingEconomics' own European wrap attributing the gain to reopening optimism, and the Euro Stoxx 50 rose 0.41% to 6298. Then on Saturday President Trump rejected it from the White House. 'That deal would not be acceptable', he said, adding that Iran wants a deal because 'they are losing so badly' and, on the decision to close the strait, 'so they outsmarted themselves. They said, let's close it and cause a problem for the world.' The Wall Street Journal reported he told aides he expects a renewed bombing campaign on Iran after the US midterm elections in November. Araghchi answered on Telegram that Iran stands by its conditions, that it awaits official communication through mediators rather than press remarks, and that 'only a negotiated solution can get them out of this deadlock'. Al Jazeera's correspondent called the proposal dead in the water. Two things make this worse than a simple return to the status quo. The first is that the escalation now has a date rather than a fade: an expectation of renewed bombing after November converts an open-ended risk premium into a scheduled one, which is a different thing for a forward curve than generic uncertainty. The second is Yanbu. The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted six ballistic missiles on Thursday aimed at Taif and the Yanbu area, and the Houthis then claimed attacks on a sensitive target in Riyadh and on Saudi Aramco facilities at Yanbu, using ballistic and cruise missiles and drones; an emergency alert covered areas including Jeddah and Mecca. Yanbu is the main alternative route for Saudi crude, fed by an East-West pipeline rated at up to seven million barrels a day - the designated bypass for a closed strait. Threatening the bypass while the strait is shut is a materially worse supply picture than threatening the strait alone, and independent trackers already put Hormuz throughput at 3.7 to 8m b/d against roughly 20m normally, around 20% of global seaborne oil trade. The FX transmission is the mirror image of what this page published yesterday, and stating that plainly is more useful than dressing it up. Four central banks have hawkish cases built explicitly on expensive energy, and all four get their condition back. Bailey said on Friday it is 'going to get harder to maintain that stance the longer we have high energy prices'; that was a liability twenty-four hours ago and is now a commitment, with three of nine MPC members already voting to hike, so GBP goes to +2. The euro-area case is the same in substance and the data is louder than the narrative: energy inflation accelerated to 14.3% y/y in August from 10.3% in July, the September flash on Friday carries a 3.7% headline consensus, and German preliminary CPI on Wednesday is forecast at 0.5% m/m from 0.2%, so EUR returns to +1 - capped only because German GfK at -30.6 leaves the Governing Council genuinely split near 53% for no change. RBNZ Governor Breman's crude-overshoot warning is restored too, though his own Bank has moved its hike to December, which is why NZD still goes to -1. And the correction this page owes: Australia is not the exception it was described as. Governor Bullock told a parliamentary committee that some of the upside inflation risks flagged in August appear to be materialising, with the rise in global oil prices reported as a driver and Brent's move from around US$80 to above US$100 cited - so the RBA case is energy-exposed like the others. The difference is direction, and today direction favours it: escalation reinforces Tuesday's hike instead of being beside the point, which is a sturdier position than the one claimed yesterday rather than a weaker one. On the other side, Canada stops being the clean loser and becomes the clean beneficiary, because rising crude improves its terms of trade and brings Macklem's US$100 conditional back within reach - so CAD goes from -1 to 0, capped by employment at -41.7k and the only contracting PMIs on this board. The franc recovers a haven bid and returns to 0, no higher, because a zero rate assumed to hold until 2029 bids on headlines and bleeds carry in between. Gold and silver get their premium leg back against a 2.84% real yield that has been winning, so both go long at low conviction. And the honest invalidation, stated as clearly as yesterday's was: Qatar is still mediating, Araghchi is explicitly waiting on official channels rather than on press remarks, and this same channel produced the June 17 memorandum - so a resumption can arrive as abruptly as the rejection did, which is why USOIL is long at medium rather than high conviction and why the trades this page prefers today, AUD/NZD and GBP/NZD, are the ones whose primary driver is a central bank calendar rather than a barrel.
